prompt: When does Svelte turn a component into the JavaScript that updates the page?
hint: Think about where the work happens: your computer or the visitor's.

choices.text: While the page runs, in a library the browser downloads first
choices.why: That is how React, Vue and Angular work. Svelte moves that work to the build.

choices.text: Before the browser sees it, when Vite compiles the file
choices.why: Right. The compiler runs on your computer, in development on every save and once more in the build.

choices.text: On the server only; the browser receives HTML and no JavaScript
choices.why: The compiler writes a program for the browser too, which makes the HTML live.

choices.text: When npm installs the svelte package into node_modules
choices.why: Installing only copies the compiler onto your disk. It compiles your files when Vite asks it to.

prompt: Match each name with what it is.
hint: One is a language, one a framework for whole apps, one a build tool.

pairs.right: The component language and its compiler
Pages at addresses, server data, forms, deployable builds
The server you work with and the bundler that builds

right_distractors: A library each browser downloads to read components

prompt: Why do the React, Angular, Vue and Svelte courses all build the same study planner?
hint: Lesson 20 depends on it.

choices.text: Because the planner needs features only all four together provide
choices.why: Each course builds the whole planner on its own; it needs one framework.

choices.text: So that the four apps can share one server and one database
choices.why: There is no shared server or database; each app reads its own small JSON file.

choices.text: So a comparison of the four compares like with like
choices.why: Right. Same screens and same data, so what differs is the code.

choices.text: Because a student is expected to take all four courses in turn
choices.why: The four are a fork: a student takes one of them.

prompt: A course later in the `frontend` track needs a component example. What may it assume?
hint: You took one of four options at this step.

choices.text: None of the four frameworks; the student took one, and nobody knows which
choices.why: Right, which is why the courses after the fork name no framework.

choices.text: Svelte, since it is the smallest of the four to learn
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with it; a student on React never saw Svelte.

choices.text: React, since most of the job listings a junior developer reads ask for it by name
choices.why: A student who chose Vue never took React, whatever the job listings say.

choices.text: All four, since the four courses at a fork are taken one after another, in sequence
choices.why: A fork is a choice, not a sequence.

prompt: You unpacked Node and linked it into `~/.local/bin`, and `node --version` says `command not found` in the same terminal. What do you do?
hint: When does a shell decide which folders it searches?

choices.text: Install Ubuntu's nodejs package with apt
choices.why: That adds a second, older Node, which this course refuses to run on.

choices.text: Open a new terminal
choices.why: Right. `~/.local/bin` joins the `PATH` only in a shell opened after the folder exists.

choices.text: Download the tarball again; the first copy was damaged in transit
choices.why: A damaged file fails when `tar` unpacks it, not when the shell looks for a command.

choices.text: Run the same command again with `sudo` in front
choices.why: Permissions are not the problem, and root's `PATH` does not include your home either.

prompt: Why does this course ask for 4 GB of memory in a virtual machine, where `javascript` asked for 2?
hint: What runs at the same time here that did not there?

choices.text: Svelte components are compiled into machine code, which needs more memory
choices.why: They compile to JavaScript, not machine code.

choices.text: Node 22 uses twice the memory of the Node in javascript
choices.why: It is the same Node 22.22.0 in both courses.

choices.text: A build of the planner and a browser run at the same time
choices.why: Right. Vite and Chromium together need more than a terminal does.

prompt: SvelteKit 3 refuses any Node older than version 22.___.
hint: The `Required` line of the refusal says it.

prompt: What does `look` print about a page?
hint: It is what assistive technology is given.

choices.text: A screenshot, converted to text characters
choices.why: It prints no picture at all, as characters or otherwise.

choices.text: The HTML the server sent, before any script ran
choices.why: It prints the page after the browser has run it, and as roles and names rather than tags.

choices.text: The tree of roles and names a screen reader is given
choices.why: Right: headings with levels, lists, buttons with their names.

choices.text: Every request the page made, with its status
choices.why: That is a network log; `look` prints what is on the page.

prompt: `look` prints `- button` with no name after it. What have you found?
hint: Who relies on the name?

choices.text: A button a screen reader announces as just "button", which is an accessibility defect
choices.why: Right. A control needs a name, from its text or a label, to be usable without sight.

choices.text: A bug in `look`: Playwright lost the button's text somewhere between the page and your terminal
choices.why: The tree is what the browser computed. No name there means none on the page.

choices.text: A button that has not finished loading yet
choices.why: `look` waits for the page to settle; a missing name is a property of the markup.

choices.text: Nothing; a button's name is decoration
choices.why: It is the only thing a screen reader user hears about it.

prompt: `look` fails with `Executable doesn't exist`, and `~/.cache/ms-playwright` holds other browser builds. What fixes it?
hint: Each Playwright version asks for one build.

choices.text: Point `look.mjs` at whichever of the builds already in that folder is newest
choices.why: Playwright asks for the build it was made with; another one is what it just refused.

choices.text: Run `npx playwright install` in `~/svelte-tools`
choices.why: Right. Run from that folder, it is the same Playwright asking, so it fetches the build it wants.

choices.text: Install Google Chrome from its website, so there is a browser on the system to drive
choices.why: Playwright does not look for your own browser; it uses its own copy.

choices.text: Delete `node_modules` in the planner
choices.why: `look` lives in `~/svelte-tools`; the planner's packages are not involved.

prompt: `npm install --save-___ playwright@1.63.0` writes `1.63.0` into `package.json` rather than `^1.63.0`.
hint: The same word the project's `.npmrc` gets later.

prompt: `npm install` stops with `EBADENGINE` and `Required: {"node":">=22.17"}`. What does that tell you?
hint: Read the `Actual` line too.

choices.text: npm itself is too old and has to be upgraded before anything else will install
choices.why: The requirement is about Node; npm 10.9.4 is the one that came with Node 22.

choices.text: A package was damaged in the download
choices.why: A damaged package fails its integrity check, with another code.

choices.text: The Node that ran is older than SvelteKit 3.1.0 declares it needs
choices.why: Right, and `engine-strict=true` turned the declaration into a refusal.

choices.text: The project's `.npmrc` has a typo in it
choices.why: The `.npmrc` worked exactly as written: it is what made npm refuse.

prompt: A tool you have never used fails with `does not provide an export named 'parseEnv'` from `node:util`. What do you check first?
hint: The lesson's failure had the same shape with another name.

choices.text: Whether the tool's own code has a typo in the import
choices.why: Possible, but a function missing from a `node:` module points at the Node first.

choices.text: Which Node ran it, with `node --version` and `which -a node`
choices.why: Right. A missing export from a built-in module is almost always an older Node than the tool expects.

choices.text: Whether `node_modules` is complete, by reinstalling
choices.why: `node:util` is part of Node itself and is not in `node_modules`.

choices.text: Whether the network allows the tool to download it
choices.why: Built-in modules are never downloaded; they come with the Node binary.

prompt: You start `npm run dev` and its first line says `Port 5173 is in use, trying another one...`. What is true?
hint: Vite did not fail.

choices.text: The new server stopped, and nothing is listening on any port
choices.why: It moved on and started, on another port.

choices.text: The old server was stopped so the new one could take 5173
choices.why: Vite never stops another program; it went looking for a free port.

choices.text: Another server still has 5173, and the new one is on 5174
choices.why: Right. The page you were looking at is the old server's, which is easy to miss.

prompt: At school, `npm install` fails with `SELF_SIGNED_CERT_IN_CHAIN`. What is the right response?
hint: Something between you and the internet is reading the connection.

choices.text: Set npm's `strict-ssl` to false for this one install
choices.why: That turns off the check that tells you who you are talking to, for every package fetched.

choices.text: Ask the network's owner for its certificate
choices.why: Right. Turning certificate checking off is never the fix.

choices.text: Download the packages by hand from a browser instead
choices.why: The browser crosses the same inspecting network, and you lose the lockfile's integrity checks.

prompt: Match each part of a new SvelteKit project with what it holds.
hint: Two are yours to edit, two are generated.

pairs.right: The pages, one folder per address
Files served exactly as they are

prompt: `package.json` says `"svelte": "^5.57.1"`. Two people install on different days. What can happen?
hint: What does the `^` allow?

choices.text: They get different 5.x versions, unless a lockfile pins one
choices.why: Right. That is why the course pins exact versions and keeps `package-lock.json`.

choices.text: Both get exactly 5.57.1, which the caret pins
choices.why: The caret is the opposite of a pin: it accepts any later 5.x.

choices.text: The second install fails, because that version number was already taken by the first
choices.why: Any number of people may install the same version.

choices.text: Either of them may receive Svelte 6
choices.why: A caret stays inside the major version.

prompt: You save `+page.svelte` while `npm run dev` runs. What happens?
hint: Nothing was restarted.

choices.text: Nothing until you stop the server and start it again
choices.why: Vite watches the files; restarting is not needed.

choices.text: Vite recompiles it; the open page updates in place
choices.why: Right. That is hot module replacement.

choices.text: The browser reloads the whole site and loses what you typed
choices.why: Hot replacement swaps the changed module in place rather than reloading.

choices.text: npm rebuilds the production files in `.svelte-kit/output`, ready for the next deploy
choices.why: That is `npm run build`, which is a separate command.

prompt: The `.npmrc` line that turns a package's declared Node version into a refusal is `engine-___=true`.
hint: `sv` wrote it there before you added `save-exact`.

prompt: In the client output, what did `let minutes = $state(0)` become, and why?
hint: Look at every read and write of it too.

choices.text: `let minutes = 0`, because the browser needs no tracking
choices.why: That is the server output. The browser is where the value changes.

choices.text: `$.state(0)`, a signal read with `$.get` and written with `$.set`
choices.why: Right. The compiler rewrote the variable so that it knows who reads it.

choices.text: A call to `useState`, which the runtime looks up on every render
choices.why: That is React's model; there is no render function here to call it from.

choices.text: It stayed `$state(0)`, which the browser understands
choices.why: No browser understands `$state`; it is input for the compiler.

prompt: When the button is pressed, what does the compiled client code update?
hint: Count the `template_effect` calls.

choices.text: The whole component, which is created again from the template
choices.why: The template is copied once, when the component is made.

choices.text: A virtual copy of the page, compared with the previous copy
choices.why: Nothing in the output keeps a copy of the page.

choices.text:
The text inside the `

`, and nothing else
choices.why: Right. One effect sets one text node.

choices.text: The button and the paragraph, since both are in the same template
choices.why: The button's text never depends on `minutes`, so no code touches it.

prompt: The server output wraps the value in `$.escape(minutes)`. Which situation is that protecting against?
hint: Think of a value that is text a student typed.

choices.text: A number too large for a string, which would crash the server
choices.why: Any number turns into a string; escaping is about what the text means as HTML.

choices.text: A course name containing `<b>`, which would otherwise become markup on the page
choices.why: Right. Escaped, it is shown as the characters typed.

choices.text: A slow connection that cuts the HTML string in half
choices.why: Escaping changes characters, not how the response is delivered.

choices.text: A visitor whose browser has JavaScript turned off
choices.why: The server's HTML reaches that visitor either way; escaping is about its content.

prompt: The step in which the client code finds the server's HTML already on the page and attaches itself to it is called ___.
hint: Lesson 15 opens it up.

prompt: `npm run build` prints two `building … environment` lines. What are the two?
hint: One runs where the pages are rendered.

choices.text: The server code that renders pages, and the code browsers download
choices.why: Right: `ssr` and `client`.

choices.text: A development build, and a production build
choices.why: Both are production builds; development is `npm run dev`.

choices.text: A build for modern browsers, and a second one for old ones
choices.why: There is no legacy build here; the two are server and client.

prompt: The two largest client files were 14.64 kB and 12.89 kB after gzip. How many kB is that together, to the nearest whole kB?
hint: Add them, then round.

prompt: You add forty pages to the planner. Which part of the client build grows with them?
hint: Two files are the same size with one page or fifty.

choices.text: Svelte's runtime, since each page needs its own copy
choices.why: Every page shares one runtime chunk.

choices.text: SvelteKit's router, which keeps a table of every page in its code
choices.why: The router is the same size with one page or fifty.

choices.text: The `nodes` files, one per page or layout
choices.why: Right. Each is a component compiled, and costs about what its own logic costs.

choices.text: Nothing grows, because pages are rendered on the server
choices.why: Pages are rendered on the server and also run in the browser, so each ships its code.

prompt: The build ends with `Could not detect a supported production environment`. Did it fail?
hint: Read what comes before it.

choices.text: Yes; nothing in `.svelte-kit/output` can be trusted
choices.why: The client and server builds above it succeeded.

choices.text: No; the build worked, and `adapter-auto` found no host to package it for
choices.why: Right. Lesson 15 replaces it with an adapter that produces a server you can run.

choices.text: Yes; Node 22 is not a supported environment
choices.why: The message is about hosting platforms, not the Node on your computer.

choices.text: No; it is a warning that the build ran in development mode rather than production
choices.why: It ran in production mode; the message is about adapters.

prompt: Put the life of `+page.svelte` in order, from your editor to a visitor's screen in a deployed app.
hint: The compiler comes before anything a browser does.
items: `npm run build` compiles it into a server part and a client part
The server sends a visitor the HTML it rendered
The client part hydrates that HTML in the visitor's browser
trap: Hydration needs HTML already on the page, so it comes after the server's response.

prompt: Which of these does the browser NOT receive for the `Counter` component? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare the source with the client output.

choices.text: The `$state` syntax as you wrote it
choices.why: Right. It was rewritten into `$.state`, `$.get` and `$.set`.

choices.text: Code that compares the page with a previous copy of it
choices.why: Right. There is no such code; the effect sets one text node directly.

choices.text: The markup, as a template string
choices.why: It does: `root` holds it and is copied when a `Counter` is made.

choices.text: A listener for clicks
choices.why: It does: one delegated listener handles the button.
